Yes, the story has an appropriate balance between scene and summary/exposition. 

Because the narrative spans roughly twenty years, the author effectively uses summary and exposition in the first half to compress time, establish Q's seemingly flawless character, and explain the narrator's long-standing insecurities regarding him. However, this exposition is punctuated by brief, vivid mini-scenes (such as Q making a frittata after a breakup, or the drunken confession at a senior year party) that keep the pacing engaging. Once the background is established, the story transitions into a central, dramatized scene at the hotel pool. By slowing down the narrative to show Q's awkwardness, dialogue, and physical actions (like the disintegrating napkin) in real-time, the author delivers the emotional climax of the story, which wouldn't have carried the same weight without the preceding summary.
